explanations.answer: He blesses them in a loud voice
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Solomon stands up and blesses the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice. I think a crowd that big needs a blessing with some volume behind it. It's a blessing for the people, spoken out loud for all of them.

explanations.answer: He reads them the book of the law
explanations.explanation: Close to a speech you might expect, friend, but not this one. The text says Solomon stood and blessed the whole assembly in a loud voice. A scroll never comes up in these verses. What the text gives us is a blessing spoken over the people.

explanations.answer: He names his son the next king
explanations.explanation: That would be a big announcement, but these verses don't have one. What Solomon does is stand and bless the whole assembly of Israel in a loud voice. It's a blessing for the people, not a handing off of the crown.

Yes, baker. Solomon says, "Not one word has failed of all the good promises He made through His servant Moses." Not one. He's looking at everything the LORD promised and saying every word held. That's a king with a lot to be thankful for.

It's the other way around, friend. Solomon says, "Not one word has failed of all the good promises He made through His servant Moses." He's looking at everything the LORD promised and saying every word held. Zero misses.

explanations.answer: That He never leaves or forsakes them
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Solomon asks, "May He never leave us or forsake us." He's wishing for the LORD to stay with them, the way He was with their fathers. When you've got that, you don't need a long list of other wishes.

explanations.answer: That He makes them the richest nation
explanations.explanation: Money never comes up in this blessing, friend. Solomon wishes for the LORD to be with them as He was with their fathers, and for Him to never leave or forsake them. That wish is about who is with them, not what's in their pockets.

explanations.answer: That He wins every battle for them
explanations.explanation: No battles in this blessing, baker. Solomon's wish is that the LORD be with them as He was with their fathers, and that He never leave or forsake them. It's about the LORD staying close, not about a winning record.

Yes, baker. Solomon asks the LORD to turn their hearts to Himself "…to walk in all His ways and to keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances He commanded our fathers." The heart gets turned, and the walking follows. Obedience is what that turned heart looks like on its feet.

I get the pull, friend, comfort sounds nice. But Solomon doesn't say it. He asks that their hearts be turned to the LORD "…to walk in all His ways and to keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances He commanded our fathers." That's a life of obedience.

Success is a fine word, baker, but it isn't Solomon's word here. He asks the LORD to incline their hearts to Himself "…to walk in all His ways and to keep the commandments…" What he's after is a life lived in obedience.

Careful, friend, this one's got a trap in it. Solomon asks God to uphold Israel's cause "…so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God." That's all the peoples, not just Israel. His wish reaches way past his own crowd.

That's it, baker. Solomon wants the LORD to uphold the cause of His servant and His people Israel "…so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God." All the peoples, not only Israel. The word "only" is what makes this one false.

Not quite, baker. Solomon says, "So let your heart be fully devoted to the LORD our God, as it is this day…" That "…as it is this day…" means their hearts are devoted right now. He's telling them to keep walking in His statutes and keeping His commandments.

Yes, friend. Solomon says, "So let your heart be fully devoted to the LORD our God, as it is this day, to walk in His statutes and to keep His commandments." The words "…as it is this day…" tell us the devotion is already there. He's not telling them to start, he's telling them to keep going.

That's right, baker. Solomon offers 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings to the LORD. I get nervous when I bake four dozen cookies, so these numbers make my mustache curl. That's a mighty big offering.

The text says it plainly, friend. Solomon offers 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings to the LORD. Those are real numbers, and they're big. My biggest batch of cookies looks like a rounding error next to that.

Yes, baker. The text says Solomon and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. The house is built, and now it's set apart for the LORD with these offerings. It's the moment the whole thing is given over to Him.
The house isn't getting bigger here, friend. The text says the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. That means setting it apart for Him, not adding on a new wing.
Nobody's locking up, baker. The text says the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. Dedicating a house means giving it to Him, and the doors are just getting started.

Yes, baker. The text says the bronze altar before the LORD was too small to contain all these offerings. So Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard and offered them there. I know that feeling, a batch bigger than the tray.

Age isn't the reason, friend. The text says the bronze altar was too small to contain all these offerings. That's why Solomon consecrated the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD. Small is the word the text gives us.

Nothing about heat in these verses, baker. The bronze altar was too small to contain all these offerings, and that's why Solomon used the middle of the courtyard. Small is the word. No oven mitts needed.

explanations.answer: From Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says it was a great assembly of people from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. That's a lot of ground for one crowd. I think a lot of people were glad to be there.

explanations.answer: From Bethel to the city of Jericho
explanations.explanation: Those two places don't show up in this verse, friend. The text says the great assembly came from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. Bethel and Jericho aren't in the verse at all. Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt is the stretch it names.

explanations.answer: From Gilgal to the hill of Gibeah
explanations.explanation: Not those places, baker. The text says the great assembly came from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt. Gilgal and Gibeah don't come up in this verse at all.
Close, friend, but the text says more. Solomon and all Israel kept the feast for seven days and seven more days, fourteen days in all. Seven was only the first half. That's a long party.
That's right, baker. The text says they kept the feast before the LORD "…for seven days and seven more days—fourteen days in all." So it wasn't just seven. It was double that.

That's it, baker. The text says the people went home "…joyful and glad in heart…" After fourteen days of feasting, I think they might have been tired too, but the text only tells us about the joy. They left happy.

I think they could well have been tired after fourteen days, friend. But the text doesn't say that. It says they blessed the king and went home "…joyful and glad in heart…" That's the feeling it gives us.
No sad feelings are named in these verses, baker. The text says the people blessed the king and went home "…joyful and glad in heart…" That's the feeling it gives us. They left glad.

explanations.answer: For the good the LORD did for David and Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says they were glad "…for all the good things that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel." Their joy comes from what the LORD did. That's something worth carrying home.

explanations.answer: For the gifts the king handed out to them
explanations.explanation: No gifts are mentioned, friend. The text says they were glad "…for all the good things that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel." Their joy was about what the LORD had done.

explanations.answer: For the rain that finally came on the land
explanations.explanation: Rain doesn't come up in these verses, baker. The text says they went home glad "…for all the good things that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel." Their gladness is about the good the LORD had done.
